content: Acute ST-Elevation Myocardial Infarction (STEMI) is a critical cardiovascular emergency caused by complete occlusion of a coronary artery, leading to transmural myocardial necrosis. ICD-10 code I21.3. Patients typically present with severe crushing or pressure-like chest pain radiating to the left arm or jaw, accompanied by diaphoresis (sweating), shortness of breath, nausea, anxiety, and palpitations. The pain is usually not relieved by rest or nitroglycerin. Key diagnostic findings include ST-segment elevation on 12-lead ECG in two or more contiguous leads, elevated and rising troponin I or T levels above 0.04 ng/mL, elevated CK-MB above 5 ng/mL, and wall motion abnormalities on echocardiogram. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes mellitus, hyperlipidemia, smoking, family history of coronary artery disease, obesity, and sedentary lifestyle. The differential diagnosis includes unstable angina, NSTEMI, aortic dissection (tearing pain radiating to back), pulmonary embolism (pleuritic chest pain with dyspnea), pericarditis (positional sharp pain with diffuse ST elevation), and esophageal spasm. First-line treatment requires emergent reperfusion: aspirin 325mg stat, P2Y12 inhibitor loading (ticagrelor 180mg preferred or clopidogrel 600mg), unfractionated heparin bolus and infusion, and emergent percutaneous coronary intervention (PCI) within 90 minutes of first medical contact. If PCI is not available within 120 minutes, fibrinolytic therapy with alteplase should be administered. This is a time-critical emergency where every minute of delay increases myocardial damage and mortality. Severity is critical and urgency is emergent requiring immediate cardiac ICU admission.

key_findings: ST depression or T-wave inversions on ECG
first_line_treatment: early invasive strategy within 24-72 hours based on risk
content: Non-ST Elevation Myocardial Infarction (NSTEMI) is a critical cardiovascular condition caused by partial coronary artery occlusion resulting in subendocardial ischemia without transmural infarction. ICD-10 code I21.4. Unlike STEMI, the ECG does not show ST elevation but may demonstrate ST depression, T-wave inversions, or be normal. The diagnosis relies on elevated and rising troponin levels in the appropriate clinical context. Patients present with chest pain or pressure, shortness of breath, diaphoresis, nausea, and fatigue. The pain may be similar to STEMI but can also be more subtle or atypical, especially in elderly patients, women, and diabetics. Risk stratification using GRACE or TIMI score determines the urgency of invasive management. High-risk features include elevated troponin with dynamic ECG changes, hemodynamic instability, recurrent chest pain, and GRACE score above 140. First-line treatment includes aspirin 325mg loading, P2Y12 inhibitor (ticagrelor preferred over clopidogrel), anticoagulation with unfractionated heparin or enoxaparin, and an early invasive strategy with coronary angiography within 24-72 hours based on risk. Key differentials include STEMI (requires emergent PCI), unstable angina (no troponin elevation), pulmonary embolism, myocarditis, and takotsubo cardiomyopathy. Risk factors include hypertension, diabetes, hyperlipidemia, smoking, prior coronary artery disease, and chronic kidney disease. Severity is critical with emergent urgency.

first_line_treatment: afterload reduction with ACE inhibitor or ARB
content: Acute Decompensated Heart Failure is a high-severity cardiovascular emergency involving acute worsening of heart failure signs and symptoms requiring urgent therapy, often from fluid overload or reduced cardiac output. ICD-10 code I50.9. Patients present with progressive dyspnea, orthopnea (difficulty breathing lying flat), paroxysmal nocturnal dyspnea (waking up gasping at night), peripheral edema in the lower extremities, rapid weight gain from fluid retention, fatigue, jugular venous distension, and bilateral crackles on lung auscultation. Key diagnostic findings include markedly elevated BNP above 400 pg/mL or NT-proBNP above 900 pg/mL, pulmonary vascular congestion and pleural effusions on chest X-ray, reduced left ventricular ejection fraction on echocardiogram, and S3 gallop on cardiac auscultation. Common precipitants include medication non-adherence, dietary sodium indiscretion, acute coronary syndrome, new-onset atrial fibrillation, infection, and uncontrolled hypertension. First-line treatment is IV loop diuretic therapy with furosemide 40-80mg (or 2.5 times the home oral dose), oxygen supplementation to maintain SpO2 above 94%, fluid restriction to less than 2 liters per day, sodium restriction to less than 2 grams per day, and afterload reduction with ACE inhibitors or ARBs once hemodynamically stable. Differential diagnosis includes pneumonia, COPD exacerbation, pulmonary embolism, nephrotic syndrome, and cirrhosis with ascites. Important monitoring includes daily weights, strict intake and output measurements, BMP every 8-12 hours for potassium and creatinine, and BNP trending.

first_line_treatment: rate control with beta-blocker or calcium channel blocker
rhythm control with cardioversion if hemodynamically unstable
content: Atrial Fibrillation is a moderate-severity cardiovascular arrhythmia characterized by irregularly irregular supraventricular tachycardia with chaotic atrial electrical activity and uncoordinated atrial contraction. ICD-10 code I48.91. It is the most common sustained cardiac arrhythmia, affecting millions worldwide. Patients present with palpitations, sensation of irregular heartbeat, dizziness, shortness of breath, fatigue, lightheadedness, chest discomfort, and exercise intolerance. Some patients may be completely asymptomatic and diagnosed incidentally. The hallmark ECG finding is an irregularly irregular rhythm with absence of organized P waves, replaced by a fibrillatory baseline, and variable ventricular rate typically between 100-160 bpm in uncontrolled AF. Management has two key pillars: rate control and stroke prevention through anticoagulation. Rate control is achieved with beta-blockers (metoprolol) or non-dihydropyridine calcium channel blockers (diltiazem), targeting heart rate below 110 bpm at rest. Anticoagulation decisions are guided by the CHA2DS2-VASc score: a score of 2 or more in men or 3 or more in women warrants anticoagulation, preferably with direct oral anticoagulants (apixaban or rivaroxaban) over warfarin for non-valvular AF. Electrical cardioversion is indicated if the patient is hemodynamically unstable. Important: AF of unknown duration exceeding 48 hours should not be cardioverted without 3 weeks of therapeutic anticoagulation or transesophageal echocardiography to exclude left atrial thrombus. Always check thyroid function (TSH) as hyperthyroidism can cause AF. Risk factors include age over 65, hypertension, heart failure, valvular disease, obesity, obstructive sleep apnea, and alcohol use.

first_line_treatment: reduce MAP by no more than 25% in first hour
typical_labs: CBC: check for microangiopathic hemolytic anemia
content: Hypertensive Emergency is a critical cardiovascular condition defined by severe elevation in blood pressure exceeding 180/120 mmHg with evidence of acute target organ damage affecting the brain, heart, kidneys, or eyes. ICD-10 code I16.1. This condition is distinct from hypertensive urgency, which has severely elevated blood pressure without organ damage. Patients present with severe headache, visual changes including blurry vision or scotomata, chest pain from cardiac ischemia or aortic dissection, dyspnea from pulmonary edema, altered mental status from hypertensive encephalopathy, nausea, vomiting, and in severe cases seizures. Key findings include blood pressure above 180/120 with documented end-organ damage such as papilledema on fundoscopic examination, acute kidney injury with rising creatinine, acute pulmonary edema on chest X-ray, acute stroke findings on neurological examination, or evidence of microangiopathic hemolytic anemia with schistocytes on peripheral smear. First-line treatment requires IV antihypertensive therapy in an ICU setting. The critical principle is controlled reduction: reduce mean arterial pressure by no more than 10-20% in the first hour and no more than 25% total in the first 24 hours. Overly aggressive blood pressure lowering can cause ischemic stroke, myocardial infarction, or acute kidney injury. Preferred agents include IV nicardipine infusion starting at 5 mg/hr titrating to 15 mg/hr, IV labetalol 20mg boluses, or IV esmolol for aortic dissection. Sodium nitroprusside is reserved for refractory cases due to cyanide toxicity risk. Special considerations: in cocaine-induced hypertensive emergency, avoid beta-blockers alone (unopposed alpha stimulation) and use phentolamine or benzodiazepines first.

first_line_treatment: outpatient: amoxicillin 1g TID or doxycycline 100mg BID
severe/ICU: ceftriaxone + azithromycin plus/minus vancomycin if MRSA risk
content: Community-Acquired Pneumonia (CAP) is a moderate-severity acute respiratory infection of the lung parenchyma acquired outside of healthcare settings, most commonly caused by Streptococcus pneumoniae, followed by Mycoplasma pneumoniae, Haemophilus influenzae, and respiratory viruses. ICD-10 code J18.9. Patients present with productive cough with purulent sputum, fever with chills and rigors, pleuritic chest pain that worsens with deep inspiration, dyspnea, fatigue, malaise, and tachypnea. Physical examination reveals crackles or bronchial breath sounds over the affected area, dullness to percussion, increased tactile fremitus, and egophony. Key diagnostic findings include lobar consolidation or infiltrate on chest X-ray, leukocytosis above 11,000 per microliter, elevated procalcitonin above 0.25 ng/mL supporting bacterial etiology, and elevated CRP. Severity is stratified using the PSI (Pneumonia Severity Index) or CURB-65 score to determine site of care. Treatment depends on setting: outpatient low-risk patients receive amoxicillin 1g three times daily for 5 days or doxycycline 100mg twice daily; outpatients with comorbidities receive amoxicillin-clavulanate plus a macrolide or a respiratory fluoroquinolone alone; inpatients receive IV ceftriaxone 1g daily plus azithromycin 500mg; ICU patients receive ceftriaxone plus azithromycin with vancomycin or linezolid added if MRSA risk factors are present. Procalcitonin-guided antibiotic duration can reduce unnecessary antibiotic exposure. Differential diagnosis includes acute bronchitis, COPD exacerbation, pulmonary embolism, lung cancer, tuberculosis, and heart failure with pulmonary edema. Risk factors include age over 65, smoking, COPD, immunosuppression, diabetes, and alcoholism.

Acute Exacerbation of Chronic Obstructive Pulmonary Disease (AECOPD) is a moderate-severity respiratory emergency defined as acute worsening of respiratory symptoms in a COPD patient beyond normal day-to-day variation, requiring a change in therapy. ICD-10 code J44.1. The cardinal symptoms are increased dyspnea beyond baseline, increased sputum volume, and increased sputum purulence, along with wheezing, chest tightness, tachypnea, and use of accessory respiratory muscles. Physical examination reveals decreased breath sounds, prolonged expiratory phase, diffuse wheezing, and in severe cases signs of respiratory distress with accessory muscle use and paradoxical abdominal breathing. Chest X-ray typically shows hyperinflation and flattened diaphragms; arterial blood gas in severe exacerbations shows respiratory acidosis with pH below 7.35 and pCO2 above 45 mmHg. Treatment follows a stepwise approach: short-acting bronchodilators including albuterol and ipratropium via nebulizer, systemic corticosteroids with prednisone 40mg daily for 5 days (longer courses have no additional benefit), antibiotics if sputum is purulent (azithromycin or doxycycline), supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 88-92% (avoid hyperoxia which suppresses hypoxic respiratory drive in COPD), and non-invasive ventilation with BiPAP for hypercapnic respiratory failure with pH below 7.35. BNP measurement helps distinguish COPD exacerbation from acute heart failure when the clinical picture is unclear. Intubation is reserved for patients failing NIV or with impending respiratory arrest. Common triggers include viral upper respiratory infections, bacterial superinfection, air pollution, and medication non-adherence.

symptoms: inability to speak in full sentences
typical_labs: ABG: respiratory alkalosis early, acidosis if severe
content: Acute Severe Asthma Exacerbation is a high-severity respiratory emergency characterized by progressively worsening airflow obstruction with increasing shortness of breath, cough, wheezing, and chest tightness that does not respond to initial bronchodilator therapy. ICD-10 code J45.51. Patients present with severe dyspnea, inability to speak in full sentences, diffuse bilateral wheezing, tachypnea with respiratory rate above 25, tachycardia, and use of accessory muscles including sternocleidomastoid and intercostal muscles. Peak expiratory flow below 50% of predicted value indicates severe obstruction. Critical warning signs include pulsus paradoxus exceeding 25 mmHg, a silent chest (indicating critically reduced airflow where wheezing disappears), and normalizing or rising pCO2 on ABG (indicating respiratory muscle fatigue and impending arrest). Early ABG typically shows respiratory alkalosis from hyperventilation; a shift toward normal or elevated pCO2 is ominous. First-line treatment includes continuous albuterol nebulization, ipratropium bromide nebulization, systemic corticosteroids (methylprednisolone 125mg IV or prednisone 60mg PO), magnesium sulfate 2g IV over 20 minutes for severe cases, and supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 above 93%. Intubation and mechanical ventilation are reserved for impending or actual respiratory failure. Prior intubation for asthma is the single strongest predictor of a fatal asthma attack. Differential diagnosis includes COPD exacerbation, vocal cord dysfunction, foreign body aspiration, anaphylaxis, pulmonary embolism, and pneumothorax.

first_line_treatment: systemic thrombolysis for massive PE with hemodynamic instability
content: Pulmonary Embolism (PE) is a critical respiratory and cardiovascular emergency caused by obstruction of pulmonary arteries by thrombus, most commonly originating from deep veins of the lower extremities, causing ventilation-perfusion mismatch and potentially fatal right ventricular failure. ICD-10 code I26.99. Presentation ranges from mild dyspnea to sudden cardiovascular collapse. Patients typically present with acute onset dyspnea (most common symptom), pleuritic chest pain, tachycardia, hemoptysis, syncope (suggests massive PE), unilateral calf swelling (suggests concurrent DVT), anxiety, and cough. Diagnosis follows a structured approach: calculate pre-test probability using Wells or Geneva score, obtain D-dimer if low probability (negative D-dimer below 500 ng/mL effectively rules out PE), and proceed to CT pulmonary angiography if high probability or elevated D-dimer. CT-PA showing filling defects in pulmonary arteries is the gold standard. Additional findings include RV strain on echocardiogram (RV:LV ratio greater than 1), the classic but uncommon S1Q3T3 pattern on ECG, elevated troponin indicating RV strain (prognostic), and elevated BNP indicating RV dysfunction. ABG typically shows hypoxemia with respiratory alkalosis. Treatment depends on hemodynamic status: stable PE receives anticoagulation with DOACs preferred (rivaroxaban 15mg BID for 21 days then 20mg daily, or apixaban 10mg BID for 7 days then 5mg BID); massive PE with hemodynamic instability receives systemic thrombolysis with alteplase 100mg over 2 hours plus unfractionated heparin. IVC filter is reserved only for patients with absolute contraindications to anticoagulation. Risk factors include recent surgery, immobilization, malignancy, oral contraceptives, prior DVT, thrombophilia, obesity, and long-haul travel.

first_line_treatment: SGLT2 inhibitor or GLP-1 RA if ASCVD/CKD/HF
content: Type 2 Diabetes Mellitus (T2DM) is a chronic metabolic disorder characterized by insulin resistance and relative insulin deficiency, leading to persistent hyperglycemia that over time causes microvascular and macrovascular complications. ICD-10 code E11.9. It is the most common form of diabetes, accounting for 90-95% of all diabetes cases. Patients present with the classic triad of polyuria (excessive urination), polydipsia (excessive thirst), and polyphagia (excessive hunger), along with fatigue, blurred vision, unexplained weight loss, slow wound healing, recurrent infections, and acanthosis nigricans (dark velvety skin patches indicating insulin resistance). Diagnosis requires any one of: fasting plasma glucose of 126 mg/dL or higher, HbA1c of 6.5% or higher, random plasma glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher with classic symptoms, or oral glucose tolerance test 2-hour glucose of 200 mg/dL or higher. Per ADA 2024 guidelines, metformin remains first-line pharmacotherapy starting at 500mg twice daily titrated to 1000mg twice daily, combined with lifestyle modifications including medical nutrition therapy and 150 minutes per week of moderate exercise. SGLT2 inhibitors (dapagliflozin, empagliflozin) or GLP-1 receptor agonists (semaglutide, liraglutide) should be added regardless of HbA1c if the patient has established atherosclerotic cardiovascular disease, heart failure, or chronic kidney disease. Insulin therapy is indicated for HbA1c above 10% or severe symptomatic hyperglycemia. Target HbA1c is less than 7% for most adults. Comprehensive monitoring includes HbA1c every 3 months, annual eGFR and urine albumin-creatinine ratio, annual lipid panel, annual foot examination, and annual or biennial dilated retinal examination.

first_line_treatment: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation NS 1-1.5L/hr initially
typical_labs: potassium: initially elevated, total body depleted
content: Diabetic Ketoacidosis (DKA) is a critical, life-threatening endocrine emergency characterized by the triad of hyperglycemia (glucose above 250 mg/dL), metabolic acidosis (pH below 7.3, bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L), and ketonemia due to absolute or relative insulin deficiency. ICD-10 code E13.10. DKA occurs most commonly in type 1 diabetes but can occur in type 2 diabetes during severe physiological stress. Patients present with nausea, vomiting, diffuse abdominal pain (can mimic acute abdomen), polyuria, polydipsia, altered mental status ranging from confusion to coma, Kussmaul respirations (deep rapid breathing compensating for metabolic acidosis), fruity breath odor from acetone, and signs of severe dehydration including tachycardia, hypotension, dry mucous membranes, and poor skin turgor. The diagnostic criteria include blood glucose above 250 mg/dL, arterial pH below 7.3, serum bicarbonate below 18 mEq/L, elevated anion gap above 12 (calculated as Na minus Cl minus HCO3), positive serum or urine ketones, and elevated beta-hydroxybutyrate above 3 mmol/L. Treatment follows a strict protocol: aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline 1-1.5 liters per hour for the first 1-2 hours then transitioning to half-normal saline; IV insulin infusion at 0.1-0.14 units/kg/hour (critically, do NOT start insulin until serum potassium is confirmed above 3.5 mEq/L as insulin drives potassium intracellularly and can cause fatal hypokalemia); potassium replacement to maintain levels between 4-5 mEq/L; add dextrose to IV fluids when glucose drops below 200 mg/dL to prevent hypoglycemia while continuing insulin to close the anion gap. The treatment endpoint is anion gap closure, not glucose normalization. Monitor glucose hourly and BMP every 2 hours. Always identify and treat the precipitating cause: infection, insulin non-adherence, new-onset diabetes, myocardial infarction, or substance abuse.

key_findings: delayed relaxation of deep tendon reflexes
first_line_treatment: take on empty stomach 30-60 min before breakfast
recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks and adjust
content: Hypothyroidism is a low-severity endocrine disorder caused by deficiency of thyroid hormone production, most commonly due to Hashimoto thyroiditis (autoimmune destruction of the thyroid gland), leading to decreased metabolic activity throughout the body. ICD-10 code E03.9. It is one of the most common endocrine disorders, affecting up to 5% of the population with a strong female predominance. Patients present insidiously with fatigue, weight gain despite normal appetite, cold intolerance, constipation, dry skin, hair loss and thinning, bradycardia, cognitive slowing and difficulty concentrating, depression, menstrual irregularities (menorrhagia in women), myalgias, and in severe cases myxedema (non-pitting edema). Physical examination may reveal a goiter (enlarged thyroid), delayed relaxation phase of deep tendon reflexes, periorbital edema, and non-pitting edema of the extremities. Diagnosis is straightforward: elevated TSH above 4.5 mIU/L with low free T4 below 0.8 ng/dL confirms primary hypothyroidism. Anti-TPO antibodies are positive in Hashimoto thyroiditis. Subclinical hypothyroidism shows elevated TSH with normal free T4. Associated laboratory findings include hyperlipidemia (elevated LDL cholesterol), macrocytic anemia, hyponatremia, and elevated CK. First-line treatment is levothyroxine replacement at approximately 1.6 mcg/kg/day, taken on an empty stomach 30-60 minutes before breakfast, separated from calcium and iron supplements by 4 hours. In elderly patients or those with cardiac disease, start at lower doses (12.5-25 mcg/day) and titrate slowly. Recheck TSH in 6-8 weeks after dose changes and annually once stable. Target TSH in the normal reference range.

key_findings: elevated free T4 and/or free T3
first_line_treatment: PTU preferred in first trimester pregnancy
content: Hyperthyroidism from Graves Disease is a moderate-severity endocrine disorder caused by excessive thyroid hormone production from autoimmune stimulation of the TSH receptor by thyroid-stimulating immunoglobulins (TSI), causing a hypermetabolic state. ICD-10 code E05.00. Graves disease is the most common cause of hyperthyroidism in iodine-sufficient regions. Patients present with unintentional weight loss despite increased appetite, heat intolerance and excessive sweating, palpitations from sinus tachycardia or atrial fibrillation, fine tremor of the hands, anxiety and irritability, diarrhea, insomnia, and muscle weakness. Graves-specific findings include exophthalmos (proptosis or bulging eyes from orbital inflammation), pretibial myxedema, and thyroid acropachy. Physical examination reveals a diffusely enlarged thyroid gland (goiter) often with an audible bruit from increased blood flow, lid retraction, and lid lag. Diagnosis shows markedly suppressed TSH below 0.1 mIU/L with elevated free T4 and/or free T3. TSI antibodies are positive and specific for Graves disease. Radioactive iodine uptake scan shows diffuse increased uptake distinguishing Graves from thyroiditis. First-line treatment includes methimazole 10-30mg daily as the preferred antithyroid drug, with propranolol 20-40mg three times daily for symptomatic relief of tachycardia, tremor, and anxiety. Definitive treatment options include radioactive iodine ablation or thyroidectomy for large goiters or when antithyroid drugs fail. PTU (propylthiouracil) is preferred over methimazole in the first trimester of pregnancy due to methimazole's teratogenic effects. Critical complication: thyroid storm, a life-threatening exacerbation requiring emergency treatment.

key_findings: rising creatinine >=0.3 mg/dL in 48hrs or >=1.5x baseline in 7 days
decreased urine output <0.5 mL/kg/hr for 6 hours
typical_labs: urinalysis: muddy brown casts (ATN), RBC casts (GN)
content: Acute Kidney Injury (AKI) is a high-severity renal emergency defined as a rapid decline in kidney function over hours to days, characterized by rising serum creatinine, decreased urine output, or both. ICD-10 code N17.9. AKI is classified using KDIGO staging: Stage 1 (creatinine rise 0.3 mg/dL in 48 hours or 1.5-1.9x baseline), Stage 2 (2.0-2.9x baseline), Stage 3 (3.0x baseline or creatinine above 4.0 or initiation of dialysis). AKI is categorized by etiology as prerenal (60-70% of cases from decreased renal perfusion due to dehydration, sepsis, heart failure, hemorrhage), intrinsic (25-30% from direct kidney damage including acute tubular necrosis, glomerulonephritis, interstitial nephritis), or postrenal (5-10% from urinary obstruction). Patients present with decreased urine output (oliguria below 0.5 mL/kg/hr), peripheral edema, nausea, fatigue, confusion from uremia, shortness of breath from fluid overload, and flank pain if obstructive. Key diagnostic workup includes trending serum creatinine and BUN, urinalysis (muddy brown casts suggest ATN, RBC casts suggest glomerulonephritis, WBC casts suggest interstitial nephritis), fractional excretion of sodium (below 1% suggests prerenal, above 2% suggests intrinsic), BUN-to-creatinine ratio (above 20:1 suggests prerenal), and renal ultrasound to assess for hydronephrosis (obstruction). First-line management: identify and treat the underlying cause, give IV fluids for prerenal AKI, immediately discontinue all nephrotoxic agents (NSAIDs, aminoglycosides, contrast dye, ACE inhibitors/ARBs in established AKI), relieve urinary obstruction with Foley catheter or nephrostomy, and monitor potassium closely as hyperkalemia is the most immediately life-threatening complication. Indications for emergent dialysis include refractory hyperkalemia above 6.5, severe metabolic acidosis pH below 7.1, uremic symptoms (pericarditis, encephalopathy), and refractory volume overload.

symptoms: warm extremities early progressing to cool/mottled late
first_line_treatment: 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus within 3 hours
norepinephrine first-line vasopressor if MAP <65 after fluids
content: Sepsis and Septic Shock represent a critical, life-threatening continuum of organ dysfunction caused by a dysregulated host response to infection, with septic shock additionally requiring vasopressors to maintain MAP above 65 mmHg and having lactate above 2 mmol/L despite adequate fluid resuscitation. ICD-10 code R65.20. Sepsis carries mortality rates of 20-30%, rising to 40-50% in septic shock, making early recognition and the Hour-1 Bundle critical for survival. Patients present with fever (or hypothermia in elderly/immunocompromised), tachycardia, tachypnea, hypotension, altered mental status ranging from confusion to obtundation, warm flushed extremities in early distributive shock progressing to cool mottled extremities in late shock, and decreased urine output below 0.5 mL/kg/hour. Diagnosis uses the SOFA score (increase of 2 or more points indicates sepsis) and qSOFA (altered mentation, systolic BP 100 or below, respiratory rate 22 or above — 2 or more suggests sepsis). Key laboratory findings include elevated serum lactate above 2 mmol/L (above 4 mmol/L indicates severe tissue hypoperfusion with high mortality), leukocytosis or leukopenia, elevated procalcitonin above 0.5 ng/mL supporting bacterial etiology, rising creatinine, thrombocytopenia and prolonged INR suggesting DIC, and metabolic acidosis on ABG. The Surviving Sepsis Campaign Hour-1 Bundle mandates: obtain blood cultures before antibiotics (but do not delay antibiotics for cultures), administer broad-spectrum antibiotics within 1 hour of sepsis recognition (vancomycin plus piperacillin-tazobactam for most patients — every hour of delay increases mortality approximately 7%), give 30 mL/kg IV crystalloid bolus for hypotension or lactate 4 or above within 3 hours, start norepinephrine as first-line vasopressor if MAP remains below 65 after initial fluids, and pursue lactate-guided resuscitation targeting greater than 10% clearance at 2 hours. Source control (draining abscesses, removing infected devices) is essential.

first_line_treatment: ferrous sulfate 325mg PO TID on empty stomach
IV iron if oral intolerant or severe
content: Iron Deficiency Anemia is a moderate-severity hematologic condition and the most common cause of anemia worldwide, caused by insufficient iron for hemoglobin synthesis resulting in microcytic hypochromic red blood cells. ICD-10 code D50.9. Patients present with fatigue (most common symptom), pallor, dyspnea on exertion, palpitations, dizziness, headache, pica (craving non-food substances like ice or clay), restless legs syndrome, brittle nails (koilonychia or spoon nails), angular cheilitis (cracking at corners of mouth), and glossitis (smooth swollen tongue). The classic laboratory pattern shows low hemoglobin (below 12 g/dL in women, below 13 g/dL in men), low MCV below 80 fL (microcytic), low ferritin below 30 ng/mL (the most specific test for iron deficiency), low serum iron, elevated TIBC above 400 ug/dL (the body upregulates transferrin production to capture more iron), low transferrin saturation below 20%, low reticulocyte count (inadequate marrow response), and hypochromic microcytic red cells with pencil cells on peripheral blood smear. First-line treatment is oral ferrous sulfate 325mg (65mg elemental iron) three times daily on an empty stomach with vitamin C to enhance absorption. Investigate and treat the underlying cause: in premenopausal women, menstrual blood loss is the most common cause; in men and postmenopausal women, GI blood loss must be excluded with upper and lower endoscopy to rule out peptic ulcer disease, colon polyps, or colorectal cancer. IV iron (ferric carboxymaltose) is indicated for oral iron intolerance, malabsorption, or need for rapid repletion. Red blood cell transfusion is indicated for hemoglobin below 7 g/dL or symptomatic severe anemia.

key_findings: Wells score helps stratify pre-test probability
typical_labs: BMP: renal function for drug dosing
content: Deep Vein Thrombosis (DVT) is a moderate-severity hematologic condition involving formation of a blood clot in a deep vein, most commonly in the lower extremities, with significant risk of embolization to the pulmonary arteries causing potentially fatal pulmonary embolism. ICD-10 code I82.40. Patients present with unilateral leg swelling (the most reliable sign), calf pain and tenderness, warmth, erythema, pitting edema, and distended superficial veins. The Homans sign (calf pain with dorsiflexion) is unreliable and should not guide clinical decisions. Diagnosis follows a structured approach using the Wells score for DVT to stratify pre-test probability: low probability patients get D-dimer testing (a negative D-dimer below 500 ng/mL effectively excludes DVT), while moderate-to-high probability patients proceed directly to compression ultrasonography, which is the gold standard showing non-compressibility of the affected vein. First-line treatment is direct oral anticoagulation with rivaroxaban (15mg BID for 21 days then 20mg daily) or apixaban (10mg BID for 7 days then 5mg BID), which are preferred over the traditional LMWH-to-warfarin bridge due to convenience and safety. Minimum duration of anticoagulation is 3 months for provoked DVT (clear trigger like surgery or immobilization), with extended or indefinite anticoagulation for unprovoked or recurrent DVT. IVC filter placement is reserved only for patients with absolute contraindications to anticoagulation. Differential diagnosis includes cellulitis (bilateral more often, with distinct erythema borders), ruptured Baker cyst, superficial thrombophlebitis, lymphedema, muscle strain, and chronic venous insufficiency. Risk factors include recent surgery or immobilization, malignancy, oral contraceptives, pregnancy, obesity, prior VTE, inherited thrombophilia, long-haul travel, and central venous catheters.

key_findings: meets DSM-5 criteria (>=5 of 9 symptoms for >=2 weeks)
content: Major Depressive Disorder (MDD) is a moderate-severity psychiatric condition characterized by persistent depressed mood and/or anhedonia with associated neurovegetative symptoms for at least 2 weeks, causing significant functional impairment. ICD-10 code F33.0. MDD affects approximately 7% of adults annually and is a leading cause of disability worldwide. Diagnosis requires at least 5 of 9 DSM-5 criteria present for 2 or more weeks: depressed mood most of the day nearly every day, markedly diminished interest or pleasure in activities (anhedonia), significant weight change or appetite disturbance, insomnia or hypersomnia, psychomotor agitation or retardation, fatigue or loss of energy, feelings of worthlessness or excessive guilt, diminished ability to think or concentrate, and recurrent thoughts of death or suicidal ideation. The PHQ-9 is a validated screening and severity tool (score 10 or above indicates moderate depression). Always screen for bipolar disorder (history of manic episodes) before starting antidepressants, as antidepressant monotherapy can trigger manic switch. Rule out medical causes including hypothyroidism (check TSH), anemia (check CBC), vitamin B12 deficiency, and substance use (urine drug screen). First-line pharmacotherapy is an SSRI: sertraline 50mg daily (preferred for cardiac patients) or escitalopram 10mg daily, with a 4-6 week adequate trial before switching. Cognitive behavioral therapy (CBT) is equivalent to medication for mild-moderate MDD, and combination medication plus psychotherapy is the most effective approach. Safety assessment for suicidal ideation must occur at every visit, with the Columbia Suicide Severity Rating Scale. SSRIs carry an FDA Black Box Warning for increased suicidality in patients under 25 — monitor weekly for the first 4 weeks.

symptoms: severe epigastric pain radiating to back
key_findings: lipase elevated >=3x upper limit of normal
Ranson or BISAP score for severity
first_line_treatment: NPO initially, advance diet as tolerated
cholecystectomy during same admission if gallstone pancreatitis
content: Acute Pancreatitis is a high-severity gastroenterological emergency involving acute inflammation of the pancreas, most commonly caused by gallstones (40%) or alcohol use (40%), with release of pancreatic enzymes causing autodigestion and systemic inflammatory cascade. ICD-10 code K85.9. Patients present with severe epigastric pain that characteristically radiates straight through to the back, is worse after eating, and may be partially relieved by leaning forward. Associated symptoms include nausea, vomiting, abdominal tenderness with guarding, fever, and tachycardia. Diagnosis requires 2 of 3 criteria: characteristic abdominal pain, serum lipase elevated 3 or more times the upper limit of normal (above 180 U/L — lipase is more sensitive and specific than amylase), and characteristic findings on cross-sectional imaging (CT showing pancreatic edema, necrosis, or peripancreatic fluid collections). Severity assessment uses the BISAP score (BUN >25, impaired mental status, SIRS, age >60, pleural effusion) or Ranson criteria. First-line treatment is aggressive early IV fluid resuscitation with Lactated Ringer's at 250-500 mL/hour for the first 12-24 hours (LR is superior to normal saline and reduces systemic inflammation), pain management with IV hydromorphone or fentanyl patient-controlled analgesia, initial NPO with early advancement to low-fat diet as tolerated (early oral feeding improves outcomes), and identification of etiology with right upper quadrant ultrasound within 24 hours for gallstones, lipid panel for hypertriglyceridemia, and alcohol history. Gallstone pancreatitis requires cholecystectomy during the same hospitalization for mild cases, with ERCP if concurrent cholangitis or persistent biliary obstruction. Prophylactic antibiotics have no benefit unless infected necrosis is proven.

key_findings: CT head to rule out hemorrhage
CT angiography for large vessel occlusion
MRI DWI for early ischemic changes
first_line_treatment: mechanical thrombectomy if large vessel occlusion within 24 hours
content: Acute Ischemic Stroke is a critical neurological emergency caused by acute occlusion of a cerebral artery resulting in focal brain ischemia and neurological deficit. ICD-10 code I63.9. Time is brain — approximately 1.9 million neurons die every minute during an untreated stroke. Patients present with sudden onset focal neurological deficits: facial droop, unilateral arm or leg weakness, speech difficulty (aphasia or dysarthria), vision changes (homonymous hemianopia or monocular vision loss), ataxia, vertigo, and in some cases sudden severe headache. The NIHSS (National Institutes of Health Stroke Scale) quantifies deficit severity. Diagnosis requires emergent non-contrast CT head to rule out hemorrhagic stroke (CT is negative for ischemia in the first 6-12 hours but rules out bleeding), CT angiography to identify large vessel occlusion amenable to thrombectomy, and MRI with diffusion-weighted imaging for early ischemic changes. The most critical element is determining time of symptom onset or last known well. First-line treatment: IV alteplase (tPA) at 0.9 mg/kg (maximum 90mg) with 10% as bolus and remainder over 60 minutes, administered within 4.5 hours of symptom onset in eligible patients. Mechanical thrombectomy is indicated for large vessel occlusion (internal carotid artery, M1 segment of middle cerebral artery, basilar artery) within 24 hours with favorable imaging (ASPECTS score 6 or above). Blood pressure management requires permissive hypertension: do not lower BP unless above 220/120, or above 185/110 if thrombolysis candidate. Aspirin 325mg is started within 24-48 hours (not within 24 hours of tPA). Door-to-CT target is 25 minutes; door-to-needle target is 60 minutes. Stroke unit admission improves outcomes compared to general ward care.

content: Bacterial Meningitis is a critical neurological emergency involving acute bacterial infection of the meninges with high mortality if untreated. ICD-10 code G00.9. The most common causative organisms are Streptococcus pneumoniae and Neisseria meningitidis. Patients present with the classic triad of severe headache, fever, and neck stiffness (nuchal rigidity), along with photophobia, altered mental status, nausea, vomiting, positive Kernig sign (inability to extend the knee when hip is flexed), positive Brudzinski sign (involuntary hip flexion when neck is flexed), and in meningococcal meningitis a characteristic petechial or purpuric rash. The cornerstone of management is IMMEDIATE empiric antibiotics — do not delay for lumbar puncture or imaging. Antibiotics should be administered within 30 minutes of presentation. Empiric regimen: ceftriaxone 2g IV every 12 hours plus vancomycin 15-20mg/kg IV every 8-12 hours for resistant pneumococcus; add ampicillin 2g IV every 4 hours if age above 50 or immunocompromised to cover Listeria monocytogenes. Dexamethasone 0.15 mg/kg IV every 6 hours for 4 days should be started before or with the first antibiotic dose, as it reduces mortality and neurological sequelae in pneumococcal meningitis. CT head before LP is indicated only if papilledema, focal neurological deficits, altered consciousness, immunocompromised state, or new seizure — but antibiotics must not be delayed for CT. CSF analysis in bacterial meningitis shows elevated WBC above 1000 with neutrophilic predominance, elevated protein above 200 mg/dL, low glucose below 40 mg/dL or less than two-thirds of serum glucose, and positive gram stain in 60-90%. Droplet precautions are required for suspected meningococcal meningitis. Close contacts require chemoprophylaxis with rifampin, ciprofloxacin, or ceftriaxone.

content: Acute Gouty Arthritis (Gout) is a moderate-severity inflammatory arthritis caused by deposition of monosodium urate (MSU) crystals in joints due to chronic hyperuricemia, most classically affecting the first metatarsophalangeal (MTP) joint (podagra). ICD-10 code M10.9. Patients present with dramatic acute onset of severe joint pain that often wakes them from sleep, with the affected joint becoming markedly swollen, erythematous, warm, and exquisitely tender — even light touch from a bedsheet can cause intense pain. The first MTP joint is the most common site, but gout can affect ankles, knees, wrists, and elbows. Low-grade fever may be present. The gold standard diagnostic test is joint aspiration showing negatively birefringent needle-shaped monosodium urate crystals under polarized light microscopy. Importantly, serum uric acid may be normal during an acute flare and should not be used to rule out gout. Joint aspiration also rules out septic arthritis, which is a critical differential that must always be considered in acute monoarthritis. Chronic tophaceous gout shows tophi (chalky urate deposits) on examination and characteristic punched-out erosions with overhanging edges on X-ray. First-line acute treatment includes NSAIDs (indomethacin 50mg TID for 3-5 days), colchicine (1.2mg then 0.6mg one hour later, most effective within 36 hours of onset), or corticosteroids (prednisone 30-40mg for 5 days) if NSAIDs are contraindicated. Urate-lowering therapy with allopurinol is indicated after 2 or more attacks per year, starting at 100mg daily and titrating to target serum uric acid below 6 mg/dL. Never initiate or change urate-lowering therapy during an acute flare as it can worsen the attack. Risk factors include male sex, obesity, alcohol consumption especially beer and spirits, purine-rich diet, thiazide and loop diuretics, chronic kidney disease, and metabolic syndrome.

content: Anaphylaxis is a critical, life-threatening systemic hypersensitivity reaction involving multiple organ systems, mediated primarily by IgE-dependent mast cell and basophil degranulation releasing histamine, tryptase, leukotrienes, and prostaglandins. ICD-10 code T78.2. Common triggers include foods (peanuts, tree nuts, shellfish, milk, eggs), medications (antibiotics especially penicillin, NSAIDs), insect stings (Hymenoptera), latex, and exercise. Patients present with rapid onset (minutes to hours) of urticaria and angioedema, dyspnea, wheezing, stridor from laryngeal edema, throat tightness, hypotension with tachycardia, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, diarrhea, dizziness or syncope, and a characteristic sense of impending doom. Diagnosis requires involvement of 2 or more organ systems (skin/mucosal, respiratory, cardiovascular, gastrointestinal) after exposure to a likely allergen. The FIRST and MOST CRITICAL treatment is intramuscular epinephrine 0.3-0.5mg (1:1000 concentration) injected into the anterolateral thigh — there is NO absolute contraindication to epinephrine in anaphylaxis, and delay in administration is the primary cause of anaphylaxis deaths. Repeat every 5-15 minutes if no improvement. ALL other treatments are adjuncts: IV normal saline 1-2 liter bolus for hypotension, supplemental oxygen targeting SpO2 above 95%, albuterol nebulization for bronchospasm, diphenhydramine 50mg IV (H1 blocker — adjunct only, NOT a substitute for epinephrine), and methylprednisolone 125mg IV to prevent biphasic anaphylaxis. Patients must be observed for minimum 4-6 hours (up to 24 hours if severe) for biphasic reactions occurring in 5-20% of cases. Discharge with 2 epinephrine auto-injectors and a written anaphylaxis action plan. Beta-blocker use increases anaphylaxis severity and reduces epinephrine efficacy — glucagon 1mg IV may be needed for refractory hypotension in beta-blocked patients.

remove K+ from body: Kayexalate, patiromer, furosemide
content: Hyperkalemia is a critical electrolyte emergency defined as serum potassium above 5.0 mEq/L, potentially causing fatal cardiac arrhythmias. ICD-10 code E87.5. Hyperkalemia is often asymptomatic until levels become dangerous, which is why it is frequently detected incidentally on routine blood work. When symptomatic, patients may experience muscle weakness, paresthesias (tingling), palpitations, nausea, fatigue, and in severe cases ascending paralysis. The ECG is the most important immediate assessment, showing progressive changes as potassium rises: peaked T waves (earliest sign, K+ 5.5-6.5), prolongation of PR interval, loss of P waves (K+ 6.5-7.5), widening of QRS complex, sine wave pattern (K+ >8.0), and ultimately ventricular fibrillation and cardiac arrest. Always rule out pseudohyperkalemia from a hemolyzed blood specimen by repeating the test. Treatment follows a structured approach based on severity and ECG findings. If ECG changes are present: give IV calcium gluconate 10% 10mL over 2-3 minutes immediately — this stabilizes the cardiac membrane but does NOT lower potassium. To shift potassium intracellularly: regular insulin 10 units IV with dextrose 50% 25g (always give glucose with insulin to prevent hypoglycemia), nebulized albuterol 10-20mg, and sodium bicarbonate if metabolic acidosis is present. To remove potassium from the body: sodium polystyrene sulfonate (Kayexalate), patiromer or sodium zirconium cyclosilicate (newer potassium binders), loop diuretics (furosemide 40mg IV) if adequate renal function, and emergent hemodialysis for refractory hyperkalemia or severe renal failure. Always discontinue offending medications including ACE inhibitors, ARBs, potassium-sparing diuretics, and NSAIDs.

content: Clostridioides difficile Infection (CDI) is a moderate-severity infectious disease involving toxin-mediated colitis caused by Clostridioides difficile, typically following antibiotic exposure that disrupts normal gut flora and allows C. diff overgrowth and toxin production (toxins A and B). ICD-10 code A04.72. CDI is the most common cause of healthcare-associated infectious diarrhea. Patients present with 3 or more unformed watery stools per 24 hours, abdominal cramping and pain, fever, nausea, and characteristically profound leukocytosis (WBC often above 15,000, sometimes above 30,000 in fulminant disease). CT imaging may show colonic wall thickening with the accordion sign in severe cases, and toxic megacolon (colonic diameter above 6cm) in fulminant disease. Diagnosis is confirmed by positive C. diff toxin assay (PCR or toxin EIA). Per IDSA/SHEA 2021 guidelines, treatment is stratified by severity: non-severe CDI (WBC below 15,000 and creatinine below 1.5) receives fidaxomicin 200mg BID for 10 days (preferred over vancomycin due to lower recurrence rate) or oral vancomycin 125mg QID for 10 days; severe CDI (WBC above 15,000 or creatinine above 1.5) receives oral vancomycin 125mg QID for 10 days; fulminant CDI (hypotension, ileus, toxic megacolon) receives oral vancomycin 500mg QID plus IV metronidazole 500mg TID, with vancomycin enemas if ileus prevents oral delivery. Critical management principles: discontinue the inciting antibiotic as soon as clinically feasible, avoid anti-motility agents like loperamide (worsen toxic megacolon risk), do NOT test for cure (PCR may remain positive weeks after clinical resolution), and consider fecal microbiota transplant (FMT) for second or subsequent recurrence (90% cure rate). The highest-risk antibiotics for CDI include fluoroquinolones, clindamycin, and broad-spectrum cephalosporins.

key_findings: Whipple triad: symptoms + low glucose + resolution when corrected
first_line_treatment: conscious: 15-20g fast-acting glucose, recheck in 15 min
unable to swallow: glucagon 1mg IM/SC or IV dextrose D50 25g
typical_labs: C_peptide: elevated in insulinoma, low with exogenous insulin
content: Hypoglycemia is a high-severity endocrine emergency defined as blood glucose below 70 mg/dL (clinically significant below 54 mg/dL), most commonly iatrogenic in diabetic patients on insulin or sulfonylureas. ICD-10 code E16.2. Symptoms follow a biphasic pattern: initial autonomic (adrenergic) symptoms include tremor, diaphoresis, palpitations, anxiety, hunger, and pallor; as glucose drops further, neuroglycopenic symptoms develop including confusion, difficulty concentrating, visual changes, slurred speech, behavioral changes, seizures, and ultimately loss of consciousness and coma. Diagnosis is confirmed by the Whipple triad: symptoms consistent with hypoglycemia, documented low blood glucose at the time of symptoms, and resolution of symptoms when glucose is corrected. For conscious patients who can swallow, give 15-20 grams of fast-acting glucose (glucose tablets, fruit juice, regular soda), recheck glucose in 15 minutes, and repeat if still below 70. For patients unable to swallow or with altered consciousness, give glucagon 1mg IM or SC, or IV dextrose 50% (D50) 25 grams. Sulfonylurea-induced hypoglycemia is particularly dangerous because these drugs have long half-lives and can cause recurrent hypoglycemia for 24-72 hours, requiring prolonged monitoring with continuous dextrose infusion and possible admission. Always identify and address the precipitating cause: insulin dose too high, missed or delayed meals, excessive exercise, alcohol use (inhibits gluconeogenesis), worsening renal function (reduced insulin clearance), or adrenal insufficiency. In non-diabetic patients with recurrent unexplained hypoglycemia, check insulin level, C-peptide, and sulfonylurea screen to evaluate for insulinoma or surreptitious insulin use.

first_line_treatment: adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100mg bolus IMMEDIATELY
typical_labs: ACTH: elevated in primary, low in secondary
content: Adrenal Insufficiency encompasses inadequate cortisol production from the adrenal glands, classified as primary (Addison disease: adrenal destruction, most commonly autoimmune) or secondary (pituitary ACTH deficiency, most commonly from chronic exogenous glucocorticoid use and abrupt withdrawal). Adrenal Crisis is the life-threatening acute decompensation. ICD-10 code E27.2. Chronic adrenal insufficiency presents insidiously with fatigue, weakness, unintentional weight loss, orthostatic hypotension, nausea, vomiting, abdominal pain, salt craving, myalgias, and hyperpigmentation of skin creases, gums, and scars (pathognomonic for primary AI due to elevated ACTH stimulating melanocytes — absent in secondary AI). Adrenal crisis presents acutely with circulatory shock (severe hypotension unresponsive to fluids and vasopressors), altered consciousness, severe abdominal pain mimicking acute abdomen, hypoglycemia, and can be rapidly fatal if untreated. Precipitants include physiological stress (infection, surgery, trauma) in a patient with undiagnosed or undertreated adrenal insufficiency, or abrupt discontinuation of chronic glucocorticoid therapy. Diagnosis: morning cortisol below 3 ug/dL is diagnostic; cortisol above 15 ug/dL excludes AI; values between 3-15 require cosyntropin (ACTH) stimulation test where cortisol below 18 ug/dL at 30 or 60 minutes confirms adrenal insufficiency. ACTH is elevated above 100 pg/mL in primary AI and low or inappropriately normal in secondary AI. Primary AI shows hyponatremia AND hyperkalemia (aldosterone deficiency); secondary AI shows hyponatremia only. Treatment of adrenal crisis: IV hydrocortisone 100mg bolus IMMEDIATELY (do not wait for diagnostic testing in suspected crisis), followed by 50mg IV every 6-8 hours, aggressive IV normal saline resuscitation (often 2-3 liters in the first hours), and IV dextrose if hypoglycemic. Maintenance therapy: hydrocortisone 15-25mg daily in divided doses plus fludrocortisone 0.05-0.1mg daily for primary AI. All patients need sick-day rules education (double or triple dose during illness or surgery) and a medical alert bracelet.

Acute Upper GI Bleeding is a critical gastroenterological emergency involving bleeding proximal to the ligament of Treitz, most commonly from peptic ulcers, esophageal or gastric varices, or Mallory-Weiss tears. ICD-10 code K92.0. Patients present with hematemesis (vomiting bright red blood or coffee-ground material), melena (black tarry stools from digested blood), or hematochezia if bleeding is massive and brisk. Associated symptoms include lightheadedness, syncope, tachycardia, orthostatic or frank hypotension, pallor, and epigastric pain. Initial assessment focuses on hemodynamic stability and risk stratification using the Glasgow-Blatchford Score (GBS): a score of 0 indicates safe outpatient management, while higher scores require hospital admission. A BUN-to-creatinine ratio above 20:1 suggests upper GI source (absorbed blood protein elevates BUN). First-line management: establish 2 large-bore peripheral IVs (16-18 gauge), initiate aggressive IV fluid resuscitation with normal saline, type and crossmatch for blood products, and transfuse packed red blood cells if hemoglobin below 7 g/dL (or below 9 if massive bleeding or cardiac disease). IV proton pump inhibitor with pantoprazole 80mg bolus followed by 8mg/hour continuous infusion for suspected peptic ulcer bleeding. If variceal bleeding is suspected (cirrhosis, known varices), start octreotide 50mcg IV bolus then 50mcg/hour infusion plus IV ceftriaxone 1g daily for spontaneous bacterial peritonitis prophylaxis. Emergent EGD should be performed within 24 hours (within 12 hours if hemodynamically unstable or ongoing active bleeding) for both diagnosis and therapeutic intervention including epinephrine injection, clip placement, or band ligation for varices. Correct coagulopathy with FFP or vitamin K if INR above 2 with active bleeding. After successful hemostasis, resume aspirin at 3-5 days if cardioprotective indication exists.

first_line_treatment: thiamine 500mg IV x3 days BEFORE glucose
DTs: high-dose benzodiazepines, ICU, consider phenobarbital
content: Alcohol Withdrawal Syndrome is a high-severity psychiatric and medical emergency encompassing a spectrum of symptoms occurring after cessation or reduction of heavy prolonged alcohol use, ranging from mild tremor to life-threatening delirium tremens, caused by CNS hyperexcitability from GABA receptor downregulation and glutamate receptor upregulation during chronic alcohol exposure. ICD-10 code F10.239. Symptoms follow a predictable timeline: minor withdrawal with tremulousness, anxiety, insomnia, diaphoresis, tachycardia, hypertension, and nausea at 6-24 hours; alcoholic hallucinations (visual, tactile, or auditory with intact sensorium) at 12-48 hours; withdrawal seizures (generalized tonic-clonic, often multiple) at 12-48 hours; and delirium tremens (confusion, agitation, fever, hemodynamic instability, mortality 5-15% untreated) at 48-96 hours. The CIWA-Ar (Clinical Institute Withdrawal Assessment for Alcohol) score guides treatment: scores above 8 indicate moderate withdrawal requiring pharmacotherapy, and scores above 20 indicate severe withdrawal. First-line treatment is symptom-triggered benzodiazepines: chlordiazepoxide 25-50mg or diazepam 10-20mg hourly as needed based on CIWA score. Lorazepam is preferred in patients with hepatic disease as it has no active metabolites requiring hepatic metabolism. Critical: administer thiamine 500mg IV for 3 days BEFORE any glucose-containing solutions to prevent precipitating Wernicke encephalopathy (confusion, ataxia, ophthalmoplegia). Also give folate 1mg daily, multivitamin, magnesium sulfate 2g IV (hypomagnesemia is nearly universal), and IV fluids for hydration. Delirium tremens requires high-dose benzodiazepines, ICU admission, and phenobarbital or propofol for refractory cases. Withdrawal seizures are treated with benzodiazepines, NOT phenytoin, which is ineffective in alcohol withdrawal seizures. Prior withdrawal episodes and prior seizures or DTs are the strongest predictors of severe withdrawal (kindling phenomenon).

symptoms: diffuse bleeding from IV sites and mucosal surfaces
first_line_treatment: FFP for prolonged PT/aPTT with bleeding
content: Disseminated Intravascular Coagulation (DIC) is a critical hematologic emergency involving systemic activation of the coagulation cascade leading to widespread microvascular thrombosis with simultaneous consumption of clotting factors and platelets, causing the paradox of concurrent bleeding and thrombosis. ICD-10 code D65. DIC is always secondary to an underlying trigger, with sepsis being the most common cause, followed by major trauma, obstetric complications (placental abruption, amniotic fluid embolism), malignancy (especially acute promyelocytic leukemia), transfusion reactions, and snake envenomation. Patients present with diffuse bleeding from IV sites, surgical wounds, and mucosal surfaces, petechiae and purpura, large ecchymoses, organ dysfunction from microvascular thrombosis (renal failure, respiratory failure, hepatic dysfunction), digital ischemia or gangrene, and altered mental status. The diagnosis is confirmed by the ISTH DIC score (5 or above): prolonged PT and aPTT, low fibrinogen below 200 mg/dL (often below 100 in severe DIC), markedly elevated D-dimer and fibrin degradation products, thrombocytopenia with rapidly falling platelet count often below 100,000, and schistocytes (fragmented red blood cells) on peripheral blood smear indicating microangiopathic hemolytic anemia, with elevated LDH and low haptoglobin. The MOST IMPORTANT treatment principle is identifying and treating the underlying cause — DIC will not resolve until the trigger is controlled. Supportive measures include platelet transfusion if count is below 20,000 or if actively bleeding, cryoprecipitate to replenish fibrinogen if below 100 mg/dL, fresh frozen plasma for prolonged PT/aPTT with active bleeding, and packed red blood cells for anemia. Heparin is considered ONLY in certain situations such as chronic DIC with thrombosis predominance or malignancy-associated DIC. Antifibrinolytic agents like tranexamic acid should generally be avoided as they may worsen microvascular thrombosis.
